posts.theme: Federal grand jury hears evidence in the Ilhan Omar investigation
posts.quote: A Federal Grand Jury Is Hearing Evidence In The Ilhan Omar Case. She Has Not Been Charged.
posts.alt: Official portrait photo of Rep. Ilhan Omar, in a floral hijab and dark jacket before a U.S. flag. Headline text: A Federal Grand Jury Is Hearing Evidence In The Ilhan Omar Case. She Has Not Been Charged. Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credit: Official portrait, U.S. House.
posts.caption:
A federal grand jury is now hearing evidence in the investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar.

That is the step that comes before an indictment. It is also the step that can end with no charges at all. Prosecutors, in newly unsealed court records, called this a "pre-indictment investigation." Omar has not been charged. She has denied any wrongdoing.

Fox News, citing sources, said there are at least two active probes. One is about alleged immigration fraud. The other is about her finances.

The court file already looks unusual. A Justice Department brief identifies her as Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, also known as Ilhan Abdullahi Omar. A warrant return left at her Washington home used a third version: Ilhan Nur Said Elmi Mohamed. The records do not explain the differences.

Investigators are looking at whether a false name or birthdate was used to get U.S. citizenship, Fox News reported. Omar says she was born Oct. 4, 1982. That date would have made her 17 when her father naturalized in 2000, still a minor, and able to get citizenship through him. Older public profiles listed 1981. That would have made her 18. After she entered Congress, her staff told outlets the 1981 year was a mistake.

Federal agents searched her Washington home in October. They took a phone, a laptop, notebooks, and a passport. Prosecutors told a court they were seeking evidence of violations "between 1980 and the present." One filing, quoted by Fox News, Roll Call, and CBS News, said: "The United States believes ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades." The same sentence said this began "long before she was ever in Congress."

A grand jury can sit for a long time and still return nothing. But this is no longer just a sealed warrant and a press statement. A grand jury is hearing the evidence.
posts.first:
The facts: Newly unsealed court records describe a "pre-indictment investigation" of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. Fox News, citing sources, reported on Nov. 25 that a federal grand jury is hearing evidence. The New York Post, also citing sources, reported a grand jury had been empaneled. Fox placed the panel in Minnesota; the Post placed it in Washington, D.C. That location is not settled here. Fox, citing sources, said there are at least two probes, one into alleged immigration fraud and one into finances. Omar has not been charged and has denied wrongdoing. A Justice Department brief identifies her as Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, also known as Ilhan Abdullahi Omar. A warrant return used a third name, Ilhan Nur Said Elmi Mohamed. Fox reported investigators are examining whether a false name or birthdate was used to obtain citizenship. Omar's official biography lists a birth date of Oct. 4, 1982.

Sources: Fox News, New York Post, Daily Wire, Roll Call, CBS News, Associated Press (unsealed search records).

posts.theme: Judge upholds Mamdani rent freeze, calls the campaign promise reckless
posts.quote: A Judge Upheld Mamdani's Rent Freeze, Then Called His Promise Reckless.
posts.alt: Photo of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a dark suit and tie, looking toward the camera. Headline text: A Judge Upheld Mamdani's Rent Freeze, Then Called His Promise Reckless. Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credit: NYC Mayor's Office, CC BY 3.0.
posts.caption:
A judge left Mayor Mamdani's rent freeze in place. Then he called the campaign promise behind it "reckless and irresponsible."

Judge Brendan Lantry wrote that the mayor "has no authority" to freeze rents. That power belongs to the Rent Guidelines Board alone. Mamdani called the ruling a victory for tenants. He did not answer the rebuke.
posts.first:
The facts: Lantry dismissed the landlords' lawsuit and left the board's 0% rent-stabilized increases in place.

Sources: Courthouse News, NY Post, amNY.

posts.theme: DOJ faces more than 97,000 ICE detainee lawsuits
posts.alt: Official portrait photo of Attorney General Todd Blanche in a circle on a dark navy bulletin graphic. Large headline text: 97,000 ICE Detainee Lawsuits. Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credit: Official portrait, U.S. Department of Justice.
posts.caption:
The Justice Department has been hit with more than 97,000 habeas corpus petitions from ICE detainees since January 2025. Close to 10,000 of those came in since October. Before this administration, federal courts typically saw a few hundred in a year.

Attorney General Todd Blanche is pulling civil lawyers in to help. His memo directs attorneys from the Antitrust, Civil, Civil Rights, and Environment and Natural Resources divisions, plus the U.S. Trustees Program, to assist U.S. Attorneys' Offices he says have been "overwhelmed." The department has roughly 2,000 civil litigators. The memo does not say how many will be assigned.

Blanche called the filings "frivolous." He wrote that the increase came, in part, from "the immigration bar's attempt to thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security."

Immigration lawyers say the numbers exploded because the administration narrowed bond hearings, so detainees went straight to federal court. Blanche says the filings are a stall tactic. Either way, 97,000 cases is not a paperwork glitch. It is a second front in the deportation fight, and the attorney general just called in reinforcements.
posts.first:
The facts: A Nov. 24 Blanche memo, reported by CBS News, the Washington Examiner, and Fox News, cited more than 97,000 habeas filings since January 2025, including about 10,000 since October. The memo does not say how many of the department's roughly 2,000 civil lawyers will be used. "Frivolous" is Blanche's word.

Sources: CBS News, Washington Examiner, Fox News.
